A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Adaptive Width Neural Networks. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added material in v3.

before.justification: v2 reports original AWNN experiments on synthetic, image, graph, and translation tasks, together with initialization, stability, and compression analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds PMNIST experiments, NAS comparisons, and additional truncation comparisons.

M1.justification: Recurrent applications are future work in v2 Section 3.3, whereas v3 Section 4 reports an implemented adaptive RNN. This adds a model instantiation; the ELBO objective, activation rescaling, quantile-based width updates, initialization scheme, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 extends evaluation into sequential classification through Permuted MNIST with an RNN. This introduces different input-processing requirements from the retained ResNet-based MNIST image task. All previous synthetic, image, graph, and translation coverage remains.

E2.justification: v3 substantially broadens comparisons beyond the retained fixed/grid-search and Fixed+ models. Appendix L evaluates random search, local search, and Bayesian optimization on the image datasets. Figure 5 also adds random and activation-magnitude-based truncation comparators absent from v2 Figure 6.

E3.justification: The new NAS comparison specifies a budget of five configurations and widths between zero and 512. The added PMNIST experiment uses the MNIST split. Previously reported splits and training settings remain unchanged; early stopping mentioned in v3's main text was already documented in v2 Appendix C.

E4.justification: v3 Figure 5 adds a focused test of whether ordered truncation outperforms random selection and selection by unscaled activation magnitude. v2 Figure 6 showed only AWNN truncation. The existing initialization, batch-size, starting-width, activation-function, and Fixed+ analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain ten-run means and standard deviations for the principal results. No additional run counts, seed specifications, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures are introduced. The new NAS table supplies no uncertainty estimates for local search or Bayesian optimization.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 and Fixed+ values remain unchanged, but substantial new comparisons are reported. PMNIST accuracy is 95.7 (0.2) for AWNN versus 91.1 (0.4) for Fixed. Table 6 adds NAS scores, and Figure 5 shows AWNN truncation outperforming its new controls. Reported maximum overhead also changes from 10x to 3–4x, without a matched timing comparison establishing a speedup.

T1.justification: New Appendices A–D introduce formal distribution-family definitions, quantile reasoning, a full ELBO derivation with an argument concerning nondifferentiable points, and a claimed Lipschitz-continuity result with proof. The existing initialization theorem and extended derivation move from Appendix A to E without substantive revision.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction expand the demonstrated applicability claim to sequences and RNNs. The principal claims about unbounded width learning through backpropagation, adaptation to task difficulty, and inexpensive compression remain. The conclusion slightly qualifies the Transformer result from the same loss to a similar loss.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 revises the overhead discussion from a naive implementation costing up to 10x to a current implementation costing 3–4x on the smallest datasets, with a more optimistic applicability assessment. Section 3.1 newly qualifies regularization and bounded activations as potentially unnecessary in practice.

D1.justification: v3 discloses hardware: 128 cores, 1.5 TB RAM, and four NVIDIA A40 GPUs with 46 GB memory. Appendix B explicitly describes using the ceiling of the continuous quantile to determine width, and Section 4 states that reproduction code is supplied in supplementary material. PMNIST-specific settings remain incompletely tabulated.

R1.justification: v3 adds references and discussion concerning dynamic networks, dynamic pruning, and width-search work including AOWS and BCNet. Appendix A further distinguishes its distribution requirements from Nazaret and Blei. The central positioning of AWNN as complementary to NAS and pruning remains.

P1.justification: v3 edits passages throughout the introduction, method, and results while retaining the six-section narrative and much of the original prose. Numbered results subsections become run-in headings, explanatory appendices precede the retained supplements, and a conference checklist is appended.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column main text to a single-column layout, with widespread resizing and repositioning of equations, tables, and figures. v3 adds the quantile illustration and NAS table and redraws the truncation plot with comparator curves. The standalone initialization plot disappears from the main text, but its content remains in appendix Figure 7.

improvement.justification: PMNIST, NAS comparisons, truncation controls, and hardware disclosures strengthen empirical coverage and documentation. However, v3 introduces mathematical problems absent from v2's corresponding material: Definition A.2 simultaneously requires bounded support and positive probability at every positive integer, while Proposition D.1's proof incorrectly infers Lipschitz continuity from almost-everywhere continuity and does not establish a uniform bound as width changes. These empirical benefits and weaknesses in the new theoretical justification prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
